cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Level 2
cards.body: International healthcare environments expect nurses caring for higher-acuity adults to use structured assessment, interpret clinical trends, apply evidence-based pathways and communicate urgent concerns with confidence.

bullets.label: This level bridges national preparation with
bullets.text: This level bridges national preparation with international acute-care expectations — strengthening advanced clinical judgement across emergency, ward and high-dependency settings.

bullets.label: Apply internationally recognised frameworks for assessment and escalation
ECGs, arterial blood gases and laboratory trends
Manage competing problems in unstable patients

cards.title: Core Competencies at a Glance
cards.body: Cardiovascular & Respiratory

bullets.label: Manage acute conditions with evidence-based nursing action
Use infusions and emergency medicines safely within scope
Lead and coordinate in high-acuity multidisciplinary settings
Support patients and families with clarity and compassion

cards.title: Why This Learning Matters
cards.body: The International Standard

bullets.label: International practice requires nurses to
bullets.text: International practice requires nurses to explain the clinical significance of findings, anticipate likely complications and escalate with a clear recommendation.

bullets.label: By completing Level 2, you will provide
bullets.text: By completing Level 2, you will provide evidence-informed nursing care for complex and unstable adults — meeting international expectations for communication, accountability and multidisciplinary practice.

bullets.label: Safe care combines protocols with professional judgement, not waiting for a single severe abnormality.

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 5 · Advanced Adult Nursing Care — Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II

cards.title: Programme Overview
cards.body: GNPS Programme 5 prepares internationally qualified nurses to interpret complex clinical data, integrate findings with bedside assessment, and act decisively in acute-care settings.

cards.title: Section 1: Interpreting Complex Clinical Data
cards.body: Acute-care nurses are expected to combine bedside assessment with diagnostic and monitoring data. Results must always be interpreted in relation to the patient, the trend, and the treatment plan — never in isolation.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: ECG, ABG, and laboratory results read with clinical accuracy
Connect what the data shows to what is happening in the body
Identify critical values and act within scope and timeframes
Explain clinical significance using structured tools like ISBAR

cards.title: Core Concepts at a Glance
cards.body: Imaging & Bedside Data

bullets.label: Each domain contributes a critical layer of
bullets.text: Each domain contributes a critical layer of information. Skilled nurses integrate all four to build a complete clinical picture and detect deterioration early.

cards.title: ECG and Rhythm Interpretation
cards.body: Within your scope of practice, you should confidently recognise:

bullets.label: Determine whether rate is normal, fast, or slow — and whether rhythm is regular or irregular.
Identify high-risk rhythms: VF, VT, complete heart block, ST elevation, and acute changes.
Clinical symptoms and the patient's haemodynamic status determine the urgency of your response.

cards.title: Arterial Blood Gases (ABG)
cards.body: ABG analysis helps identify respiratory and metabolic disturbances. Focus on four key parameters:

bullets.label: Always assess ABG results alongside the
bullets.text: Always assess ABG results alongside the patient's work of breathing and serial trends — a single result in isolation can be misleading.

cards.title: Laboratory Trends: What to Watch
cards.body: Key laboratory panels signal deterioration or treatment risk. Monitor trends over time, not just single readings.

bullets.label: Sodium, potassium, magnesium — imbalances drive arrhythmias and neurological changes.
Creatinine, urea, bilirubin, ALT — early markers of organ stress.
Haemoglobin, WBC, platelets and INR guide transfusion and bleeding risk decisions.
Troponin confirms myocardial injury; lactate reflects tissue perfusion and sepsis severity.

cards.title: Imaging and Bedside Monitoring
cards.body: Diagnostic imaging and bedside technology provide essential contextual data:

bullets.label: Chest X-ray — fluid, consolidation, pneumothorax, line placement
CT findings — emboli, haemorrhage, abdominal pathology
Ultrasound — cardiac function, fluid status, effusions
Continuous monitoring — SpO₂, EtCO₂, invasive pressures
Technology supports — but never replaces — direct clinical examination.

cards.title: Integrating the Four Data Domains
cards.body: Skilled interpretation means drawing on all four domains simultaneously — no single result tells the whole story.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Recognising Respiratory Decompensation
cards.body: An IQN is caring for a breathless patient. Serial ABGs reveal:

bullets.label: Indicates ventilatory failure and CO₂ retention
Respiratory acidosis — the body can no longer compensate
The nurse recognises respiratory
bullets.text: The nurse recognises respiratory decompensation, communicates the trend using ISBAR, and prepares for escalation to higher-level respiratory support.

cards.title: Applying ISBAR in Clinical Escalation
cards.body: Recommendation

bullets.label: ISBAR ensures that critical clinical
bullets.text: ISBAR ensures that critical clinical information is communicated in a structured, concise, and safe manner — essential when escalating a deteriorating patient.

cards.title: Interpreting Results in Clinical Context
cards.body: A result is only meaningful when placed in context. Always ask three questions:

bullets.label: Compare current values with the patient's prior results — a "normal" value may be abnormal for this individual.
Is the value improving, deteriorating, or stable? Trajectory often matters more than a single data point.
What does it mean for this patient right now?
Integrate results with the clinical assessment and current treatment plan to determine the appropriate response.

cards.title: Escalating Critical Values
cards.body: When critical values are identified, a structured response is essential:

bullets.label: Identify that the value is outside safe limits or represents a significant change.
Initiate immediate bedside assessment and any urgent nursing interventions.
Use ISBAR to communicate urgently with the medical or senior nursing team.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Interpret in Context

bullets.label: Results mean nothing without the clinical picture.
Compare against baseline and monitor trajectory.
Critical values require immediate, structured communication.
Explain what the result means for the patient's immediate care.

decks.title: Managing High-Risk Therapies & Acute Interventions
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 5 - Level 2 - Section 2 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Advanced Adult Nursing Care
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 5 · Section 2

bullets.label: Managing High-Risk Therapies and Acute Interventions — Level 2: International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: Higher-acuity adults frequently require complex, high-risk interventions. Safe nursing practice depends on competence, independent checks, close monitoring, and clear escalation pathways.

bullets.label: Bleeding risk, coagulation monitoring & drug interactions
Rapid-acting drugs with serious adverse risk profiles

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be equipped to practise safely across high-acuity clinical settings.

bullets.label: Apply safe practice within your professional scope, including accurate programming and access assessment.
Identify treatment complications early and link new symptoms to possible pharmacological causes.
Interpret clinical data and laboratory results to inform timely nursing decisions.
Seek supervision for unfamiliar therapies and escalate urgently when patient safety is at risk.

cards.title: Intravenous Infusions
cards.body: Controlled IV administration is a cornerstone of high-acuity nursing. Errors can be life-threatening — precision is non-negotiable.

bullets.label: Vasoactive agents, antiarrhythmics, insulin
bullets.text: Vasoactive agents, antiarrhythmics, insulin infusions, and electrolyte replacements all require careful titration and continuous monitoring.

bullets.label: Confirm rate, concentration, and dose with an independent check before initiating or adjusting any infusion.
Verify appropriate IV access, assess the insertion site regularly, and document patient response at defined intervals.

cards.title: Anticoagulation & Bleeding Risk
cards.body: Anticoagulant therapy carries inherent bleeding risk requiring vigilant monitoring of coagulation results, haemodynamic status, and drug interactions.

bullets.label: Monitor INR, APTT, anti-Xa levels as indicated by protocol
Assess for overt and covert signs of bleeding at every assessment
Check for interactions with NSAIDs, antibiotics, and herbal agents
Unexpected neurological change or sudden severe headache = immediate escalation
Sudden neurological deterioration in an anticoagulated patient is a medical emergency. Act immediately.

cards.title: Oxygen & Ventilatory Support
cards.body: Choosing the right oxygen delivery device — and monitoring its effect — is a critical nursing responsibility in the management of hypoxaemic patients.

bullets.label: Nasal cannula (1–6 L/min) and simple face mask — suitable for mild hypoxia. FiO₂ varies with respiratory effort.
Venturi mask delivers precise FiO₂. High-flow nasal cannula provides heated, humidified oxygen at up to 60 L/min.
CPAP and BiPAP support patients with respiratory fatigue. Monitor comfort, mask seal, and skin integrity closely.
Assess SpO₂, RR, work of breathing, ABG trends, and signs of fatigue or deterioration continuously.

cards.title: Emergency Medicines
cards.body: Emergency medications act rapidly — and carry serious risks. Nurses must be prepared before administering, not after.

bullets.label: Verify the clinical indication, patient allergies, and prescriber order before drawing up any emergency agent.
Calculate weight-based doses carefully. Confirm the correct route — IV, IM, or oral — and concentration.
Anticipate adverse effects. Ensure resuscitation equipment is immediately accessible before administration.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Anticoagulant Emergency
cards.body: "A patient receiving anticoagulation develops a sudden severe headache and unilateral weakness."

bullets.label: Perform rapid neurological exam and vitals
Notify medical team and stroke/emergency response
Arrange CT and reversal treatment readiness
This scenario illustrates how rapidly new
bullets.text: This scenario illustrates how rapidly new symptoms must be linked to active therapies. The nurse's speed and structured response can be the difference between recovery and permanent harm.

cards.title: Key Monitoring Principles
cards.body: High-Risk = High Vigilance

bullets.label: The complexity of a therapy must be matched by the intensity and frequency of nursing assessment.
Always use a second-nurse verification for high-risk medications, infusion pump programming, and dose calculations.
New or changing symptoms should immediately prompt a review of all active medications and infusions.
Never operate unfamiliar equipment without orientation. Seek supervision — this is a sign of professional strength.

cards.title: Manage Complexity with Confidence
cards.body: Section 2 equips you to care for high-acuity adults safely — from IV titration to emergency response.

bullets.label: Questions will test your ability to prioritise, escalate, and apply the nursing process under high-stakes conditions.
Complete the section assessment, review medication protocols, and practise clinical scenarios with your study group.
Competence in high-risk therapy management is a
bullets.text: Competence in high-risk therapy management is a defining skill for internationally qualified nurses seeking registration and NCLEX success.

cards.title: Multidisciplinary Coordination, Delegation and Escalation
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 5 · Section 3

bullets.label: Advanced Adult Nursing Care — Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: Managing Complexity with Confidence

bullets.label: Complex adults require coordinated input from
bullets.text: Complex adults require coordinated input from nursing, medicine, respiratory therapy, pharmacy, critical care and beyond. The registered nurse remains the anchor — responsible for assessment, prioritisation, evaluation and appropriate delegation throughout every episode of care.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: After completing this section, you should be able to:
Work confidently alongside medicine, pharmacy, respiratory and critical care during high-acuity events
Match tasks to patient need, activity type and the competence of the team member receiving the task
Apply read-back techniques in emergencies, resuscitation and for verbal medication orders
Prepare, handover and maintain care until responsibility is formally accepted at the receiving team

cards.title: Core Concept: Team Roles
cards.body: Clear, defined roles reduce duplication, prevent missed care and improve patient safety outcomes. As the registered nurse, you must know who is leading, what has been completed and what remains outstanding at all times during a clinical event.

bullets.label: Confirm who holds clinical authority and overall coordination responsibility
Maintain situational awareness of actions assigned, in progress and completed
Speak up when tasks are unclear, unassigned or delayed — silence is a patient safety risk

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Safe Delegation: Know the Boundaries

bullets.label: Delegation is permitted only when three
bullets.text: Delegation is permitted only when three conditions are met — the right patient, the right activity and the right worker competence. When in doubt, retain the task.

bullets.label: Routine observations and vital sign recording

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Closed-Loop Communication

bullets.label: In high-pressure situations, messages are
bullets.text: In high-pressure situations, messages are easily misheard or misunderstood. Closed-loop communication ensures critical information is received, understood and acted upon correctly every time.

bullets.label: This technique is essential during rapid
bullets.text: This technique is essential during rapid response events, resuscitation, and whenever verbal medication orders are given. A confirmed read-back dramatically reduces error under stress.

cards.title: Core Concept
cards.body: Escalation and Transfer of Care

bullets.label: Transferring a patient to a higher level of
bullets.text: Transferring a patient to a higher level of care is a high-risk event. The nurse holds responsibility until care is formally accepted by the receiving team.

bullets.label: Address immediate life threats before initiating transfer
Provide a concise, structured SBAR or ISBAR handover
Ensure equipment, documentation and medications are ready
Continue observation and intervention until formal acceptance

cards.title: Clinical Application
cards.body: Rapid-Response Event: Nurse in Action

bullets.label: During a rapid-response event, the nurse
bullets.text: During a rapid-response event, the nurse maintains clinical leadership while delegating time-sensitive but non-assessment tasks to competent team members.

bullets.label: All instructions were repeated back by team members — reducing the risk of error in a high-stress environment.

cards.title: NCLEX Focus
cards.body: Delegation: What the Exam Tests

bullets.label: NCLEX questions on delegation frequently test
bullets.text: NCLEX questions on delegation frequently test your ability to apply the Five Rights of Delegation and identify tasks that must never be delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP).

bullets.label: Is this task appropriate to delegate at all?
Does this team member hold the required competence?
Were instructions clear, complete and understood?
Is the RN monitoring and evaluating the outcome?

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Carry these four principles into every complex care situation:

bullets.label: Clarity of role prevents duplication and missed care
The RN retains responsibility for all assessment and evaluation
Use Closed-Loop Communication for Critical Information
Read-back confirms accuracy when it matters most
Maintain Care Until Transfer is Formally Completed
Never hand over until the receiving team has formally accepted

decks.title: Family Communication & Person-Centred High-Acuity Care
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 5 - Level 2 - Section 4 International Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS)
cards.body: Programme 5 · Advanced Adult Nursing Care

bullets.label: Adult Medical-Surgical Nursing II — Level 2: International Qualified Nurse (IQN)

cards.title: Manage Complexity with Confidence
cards.body: Serious illness is frightening for patients and families alike. Even in urgent, high-acuity settings, communication, dignity, and cultural safety remain non-negotiable pillars of excellent nursing care.

bullets.label: Every decision keeps the patient's values at the centre.
Families hold vital knowledge that informs safe assessment.
Beliefs and preferences are respected throughout the care journey.

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Convey complex clinical information with clarity and compassion.
Engage families appropriately in acute and high-acuity care settings.
Honour cultural identity, legal consent, and individual patient preferences.
Guide patients and families through difficult and unpredictable situations.

cards.title: Communication During Crisis
cards.body: When urgency is high, clear and honest communication becomes even more critical — not less.

bullets.label: Avoid unexplained clinical terminology. Speak
bullets.text: Avoid unexplained clinical terminology. Speak in terms the patient and family can understand without compromising accuracy.

bullets.label: Explain what is known, what is actively being done, and when further information will be available.
Urgency does not suspend a patient's right to respectful, dignified care and communication.

cards.title: The Value of Family Knowledge
cards.body: Families observe patients across time and contexts that clinical staff cannot. Their insight is a clinical asset, not a distraction.

bullets.label: Families can identify subtle changes from the patient's individual baseline
Their accounts are especially critical when the patient cannot communicate
Listen actively and without assumptions — family knowledge supports safer assessment
Document and escalate relevant family observations to the treating team

cards.title: Cultural and Spiritual Needs in Acute Care
cards.body: Cultural Decision-Making

bullets.label: Cultural beliefs shape how patients and
bullets.text: Cultural beliefs shape how patients and families approach treatment choices, touch, and family roles. Never assume — always ask respectfully.

bullets.label: End-of-life rituals, dietary requirements, and
bullets.text: End-of-life rituals, dietary requirements, and spiritual practices must be identified and honoured as part of holistic care.

bullets.label: Always use accredited professional interpreters
bullets.text: Always use accredited professional interpreters for critical and high-risk clinical discussions — never rely on family members to interpret.

cards.title: Shared Decision-Making
cards.body: Informed consent is not a single event — it is an ongoing collaborative process between clinicians, patients, and families.

bullets.label: Patients and substitute decision-makers must understand all available options
Likely outcomes, benefits, and burdens should be explained clearly
Nursing advocacy ensures the patient's values and preferences are heard and acted upon
Document shared decisions and communicate them across the care team
Advocacy is a core nursing responsibility — speak up for the patient's known wishes.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Stroke Patient
cards.body: A patient with a severe stroke is unable to communicate his wishes to the care team.

bullets.label: The nurse actively listens as the family shares the patient's previously expressed values and treatment preferences.
A professional interpreter is arranged for complex discussions, ensuring nothing is lost or misunderstood.
The nurse ensures all gathered information is formally communicated and documented for the treating team.
High-acuity situations never justify removing a patient's right to respectful, person-centred care.
For any high-risk or critical communication, a professional interpreter is mandatory — not optional.
Families provide unique clinical insight. Approach every conversation with openness and curiosity.
Represent and champion the patient's known values, preferences, and goals across the entire care team.

cards.title: Ready for Your NCLEX Journey?
cards.body: Section 4 equips International Qualified Nurses with the communication frameworks and clinical reasoning skills needed to excel in complex, person-centred care — and to succeed in NCLEX preparation.

bullets.label: Communication, advocacy, and cultural competence are high-frequency NCLEX examination domains.
Proceed to Programme 5 further sections to build Advanced Adult Nursing competence.
